question: What is the primary purpose of a nasogastric tube?

options.A: To provide continuous oxygen to the lungs
options.B: To deliver liquid nutrients directly into the stomach
options.C: To drain excess urine from the bladder
options.D: To remove harmful toxins from the bloodstream

explanation: A nasogastric tube is passed through the nose into the stomach to supply food and medications when a patient cannot swallow safely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why do we prefer feeding through a stomach tube rather than an IV drip when the patient's digestive system is working?

options.A: It keeps the gut healthy and stops bad bacteria from moving around
options.B: It is completely painless and requires no monitoring
options.C: It completely eliminates the risk of aspiration
options.D: It takes only a few minutes to set up every morning

explanation: Using the normal digestive tract keeps the gut lining strong and stops dangerous bacteria from escaping into the bloodstream. You've got this!

question: What position should your patient be in when you are inserting a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Lying on the left side (Sims position)
options.B: Sitting upright in high Fowler's position

explanation: Sitting the patient straight up aligns their throat nicely, making it much easier and safer to slide the tube down. Great job!

question: A patient needs a nasogastric tube but has a history of a severe skull fracture at the base of the head. What should you do?

options.A: Perform the insertion quickly while the patient is asleep
options.B: Proceed with normal insertion using extra lubrication
options.C: Consult the doctor because putting a tube through the nose is risky here
options.D: Insert the tube through the mouth instead without checking

explanation: A basilar skull fracture means the bone near the brain is damaged, so passing a tube through the nose could accidentally enter the brain. Always check with your senior or doctor!

question: What kind of lubricant should you put on a nasogastric tube before sliding it in?
explanation: We use a water-soluble jelly so that if a tiny bit accidentally goes into the lungs, the body absorbs it safely without causing pneumonia.

question: Why do nurses use a pH testing strip when checking a newly placed nasogastric tube?

options.A: To test how acidic the fluid pulled from the tube is
options.B: To check the expiry date of the food formula
options.C: To check if the patient has a stomach ulcer
options.D: To measure the sugar level in the feed

explanation: Stomach acid is very sour! Testing the pH of fluid from the tube helps us confirm the tip is safely inside the acidic stomach, not the lungs.

question: When measuring for a nasogastric tube using the NEX method, what does the letter 'E' stand for?
explanation: NEX stands for Nose to Earlobe to Xiphoid process. It's the classic bedside trick to guess how far the tube needs to go!

question: What should you do immediately if your patient starts coughing violently and turning blue while you are passing a tube?

options.A: Ask the patient to take a deep breath and swallow
options.B: Push the tube down faster to clear the way
options.C: Stop pushing and pull the tube right back out
options.D: Inject water to wash it down

explanation: Coughing and turning blue (cyanosis) means the tube has mistakenly slipped into the windpipe instead of the food pipe. Pull it back out immediately and let them catch their breath!

question: What is considered the absolute best (gold standard) way to confirm a nasogastric tube is in the right spot?

options.A: Measuring the length of tubing left outside the nose
options.B: Listening for air sounds over the belly with a stethoscope
options.C: Checking for water drops inside the clear plastic tube

explanation: An X-ray gives us clear visual proof that the tip is sitting comfortably in the stomach before we start any feeding.

question: Which pH test result tells you that the nasogastric tube is successfully resting in the stomach?
explanation: Stomach contents are acidic, so a low pH (like 4.0 or lower) is a strong sign that your tube is in the right place.

question: How much water is normally used to flush a nasogastric tube before and after giving feeds?
explanation: A quick flush of about 30 mL of clean water keeps the tube clear of leftover formula and prevents blocks without flooding the patient.

question: Why must the head of the bed stay raised for at least 30 minutes after a tube feeding?

options.A: To let gravity keep the food down and prevent it from flowing into the lungs
options.B: To help the stomach absorb food much faster
options.C: To keep the patient awake and chatty
options.D: To ensure the nurse can easily check the vital signs

explanation: Keeping the bed elevated uses gravity to stop the food from flowing back up into the throat and causing aspiration pneumonia. Safety first!

question: What is the best way to stop a nasogastric tube from getting blocked?

options.A: Changing the tube to a smaller size every week
options.B: Adding cooking oil to every feed
options.C: Flushing it with warm water before and after feeds and drugs
options.D: Blowing air down the tube twice a shift

explanation: Regular water flushes wash away sticky food and medicine residue before they can dry up and clog your tube.

question: A patient on continuous tube feeding has a red, sore spot right on the edge of their nostril. What should you do?

options.A: Clean the skin, apply a protective cream, and tape the tube to a slightly different spot
options.B: Put thick gauze padding under the tube
options.C: Leave the tape loose so the tube rubs freely
options.D: Pull the tube out permanently and stop feeding

explanation: Protecting the skin and shifting the pressure point gives the sore spot a chance to heal while keeping the patient fed.

question: What instruction should you give your patient right before you pull out a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Cough gently to clear the throat
options.C: Blow air out forcefully through the mouth
options.D: Take a deep breath and hold it

explanation: Holding the breath closes the windpipe, keeping the lungs safe from breathing in any leftover fluid as the tube slides out.

question: Why should you always look closely at the tip of the nasogastric tube right after removing it?

options.A: To measure the patient's stomach length
options.B: To check how much stomach acid is left on it
options.C: To make sure the whole tube came out in one piece and nothing broke off inside
options.D: To check if the patient chewed on the plastic

explanation: Checking the removed tube ensures no broken bits were left behind in the patient's stomach or food pipe. A quick glance saves a lot of trouble!
